🇲🇽💵 <u>Mexico asks the IMF for less: credit line cut to $18 billion</u>

At Mexico's own request, the IMF renewed its Flexible Credit Line for another year and cut it from $24 billion to $18 billion, the seventh reduction of a precautionary line that once reached $88 billion, El Economista reports. Hacienda and Banxico's Exchange Commission: "the Mexican authorities decided to continue the strategy of gradual and orderly reduction." The IMF board noted strengthening economic activity and inflation "close to target," and while it pushed for a faster fiscal adjustment, it said that should come without compromising priority spending on social programs and infrastructure.

🇲🇽💧 <u>Coyoacán neighbors block Tlalpan against four luxury towers</u>

Residents of Atlántida, Ciudad Jardín, Campestre Churubusco and the Multifamiliar Tlalpan blocked Calzada de Tlalpan on November 11 to demand Mexico City suspend "Skyline Coyoacán": four towers up to 15 stories, 430 apartments and 56,213 m² of construction on a 6,102 m² lot. Neighbors say it would need 450,000 extra liters of water a day, pumped from its own well out of the same aquifer their homes depend on, on lake-bed soil that left the Multifamiliar damaged in the 2017 quake. They are filing amparos to force the permits into the open, and Damnificados Unidos warns the high-end project feeds speculation, rising rents and displacement.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Sheinbaum takes Plan México to APEC in Shenzhen, and Mexico chairs APEC in 2028</u>

Sheinbaum will be at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, November 17-19: keynote speaker before the APEC Business Advisory Council of more than 1,000 executives from the 21 economies, a plenary alongside Xi Jinping, and bilaterals with China, Canada, Australia and Vietnam. Her pitch is Plan México, investment that builds national production and adds value at home. "That is the vision of our Plan México and it is part of what we are going to put forward." Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard: APEC's 21 economies are about 60% of world GDP and half of global trade, and Mexico was elected unanimously to preside over it in 2028.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Who's behind "Cuando perdimos el juicio," the documentary against Mexico's judicial reform</u>

Contralínea traces the documentary to a network of NGOs and foundations: Juicio Justo, the Due Process of Law Foundation, Réplica, NYU's Rule of Law program and Germany's Konrad Adenauer Stiftung. Juicio Justo's director Laurence Pantin came out of México Evalúa, which receives US government money through the National Endowment for Democracy. The KAS ran training programs with Norma Piña's old Supreme Court and with the PAN, and lists among its Mexican partners the governments of Guanajuato and Chihuahua, "governed by María Eugenia Campos, who opened the door to the CIA." That old Court is the one where Piña voted against the Republican Austerity Law and the Asset Forfeiture Law.

🇲🇽🌱 <u>Mexico moves to cut 2,460 tons of agrochemicals and rebuild its soils</u>

Mexico's Agriculture Ministry and the UNDP are launching two five-year projects backed by more than $20 million from the Global Environment Facility: FARM+, to reduce and manage agrochemicals, and "Forjando alianzas por el océano," against water pollution. Target: 2,460 fewer tons of agrochemicals and sustainable practices on more than 839,000 hectares, centered on rural women and Indigenous producers in Chiapas, Jalisco, Oaxaca, the Yucatán Peninsula, Sinaloa and Veracruz. Agriculture Secretary Columba López says the goal is "to recover the health of the soils, reduce contaminants, protect ecosystems." Same government that wrote the ban on GM corn planting into the Constitution.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>The Chihuahua prosecutor who worked with the CIA fled to the US, and Washington is protecting him</u>

Guillermo Zuany, Chihuahua's former strategic operations and anti-kidnapping prosecutor under PAN governor Maru Campos, has fled to the United States and is under US government protection, The New York Times reports, citing Mexican and US officials. For more than six months Zuany coordinated CIA agents training Chihuahua's forces. He left after it emerged the FGR holds arrest warrants against him; his former boss, ex-state attorney general César Jáuregui, is already jailed on treason charges. Washington had reportedly revoked his visa over suspected cartel ties, then restored it after he worked with the CIA. Sheinbaum: "It's worth knowing who this person is and how he collaborates with one of the agencies of the United States."
